tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

2	
3	# Writing the skills
4	
5	The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.
6	
7	## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else
8	
9	A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
10	- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
11	- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."
12	
13	## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them
14	
15	A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
16	- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
17	- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."
18	
19	## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest
20	
21	Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
22	- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
23	- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"
24	
25	## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work
26	
27	A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
28	- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
29	- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."
30	
31	Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.
32	
33	## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name
34	
35	A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
36	- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
37	- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."
38	
39	## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace
40	
41	The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
42	- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
43	- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."
44	
45	Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.
46	
47	## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read
48	
49	A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.

<!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

80	
81	**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).
82	
83	**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. Such a call does not run compiled yet. Until the switch-over, compiled programs do not link `NatReflect`, which is part of the interpreter's library. After the switch-over, such a call still fails, for a second reason. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, so its `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size. A compiled call fails the JVM's verification if it passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected (row 307). This holds for a program's own trait too.
84	
85	## Numbers
86	
87	**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** The record calls this choice route A. Route C is the way not chosen: a checker rule under which the number types could nest again. The record still calls the number and order traits "the tower". That word does not mean that they nest.
88	
89	**A numeral converts where it stands (P-173).** A numeral's own type is `NaturalNumeral`, or `RadixPointNumeral` with a radix point (P-174). Both lie below `Numeral`, a sibling of the number types under `Number`, and hold the numeral's exact value. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude names them `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral`. A place fixes a type when its declared type is a numeral type, or has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`, and `(h = 0.5)` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the binding runs, with 'Type mismatch binding' and the numeral. Walk gives `Infinity` for the second (row 967). Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. Elsewhere includes an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, `Index` and an unbounded type parameter. So `n = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64`, and `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`. The default stays the value's type: for `x = 0.1`, `q: QQ = x` is refused. A type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default that holds them all. A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`, so `u: NN32 = n` is refused (P-173, P-40). Such a parameter of 2^31 or more is a `ZZ64` under walk, and raises an error on the compiled path (row 962).
90	
91	Write a numeral type only as the parameter type of a coercion or an operator. The checker refuses it as the type of a variable, a field or a return (P-174). A program's own number type receives a numeral through its own `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral)` or `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`. Its body reads the numeral's getters `digits`, `fractionDigits`, `radix` and `digitValue`. A negative constant, as `-3`, reaches it as the type's prefix `-` on the coercion's result for `3`, so a type without `-` refuses it. Until the switch-over, a compiled program writes `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` or `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)`. The coercion gives one value for each place where the numeral is written, and each run of that place reuses it. Without such a coercion, the type refuses a numeral. The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or a `Matrix` only at the eight number types; at a program's own number type they give a plain array. `interpreter.md` and `compiler.md` give the other departures from these rules.
92	
93	**An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker, on both paths (P-173).** The fold covers the arithmetic operators, `^` up to the exponent 4096, `MIN`, `MAX`, the comparisons, and `DIV`, `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD`, `LCM`, `CHOOSE` and `MINMAX` over integers. It leaves alone the wrapping, saturating and bitwise operators, the shifts, a division by zero, an integer base at a negative exponent, and a result that can be `-0.0`. A folded comparison is a boolean. Any other result is one numeral, which converts as above or takes its default, or a quotient that is not whole, which stays `n / d` in lowest terms and defaults to a `QQ`. So `2147483647 + 1` is the `ZZ64` 2147483648, not an `IntegerOverflow`, `(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3)` is `true`, and under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`. `||` of string literals folds into one literal (P-171). A chain of `||` folds character literals too, if its first or second operand is a string literal. A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand: write `m: ZZ32 = 2147483647`, then `m + 1`, or `t: String = "ab"`, then `t || "c"`.
94	
95	**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts a value other than a numeral at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). The rule converts at a declared return type too, but walk does not (row 387). Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". Where the tied declarations differ only at the positions of the call's numerals, both paths read the numeral as its default.
96	
97	**An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter, as `x.asZZ32`: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The low-bits functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. On the fixed-width types, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, `narrow` and `widen` give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, `signed` and `unsigned` the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and `big` a `ZZ`. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. `ZZ` has only `big`, so for a `ZZ` value `z`, `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. Each `bitsAs…` getter equals `unsigned` or `signed`, as `bitsAsNN32` of a `ZZ32`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).

**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. Such a call does not run compiled yet. Until the switch-over, compiled programs do not link `NatReflect`, which is part of the interpreter's library. After the switch-over, such a call still fails, for a second reason. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, so its `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size. A compiled call fails the JVM's verification if it passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected (row 307). This holds for a program's own trait too.

+# What the revival changed in the team's Fortress
+
+This part gives the departures of revived Fortress from the team's Fortress, and from what you expect from Java, Scala, Haskell or Julia. The team left three forms that disagree: the specification, walk with the interpreter's library, and the compiled path with the compiler's library. The rules below resolve them. Read the part whole, after `SKILL.md`, before work.
+
+Each bold rule states the rule of this tree. A sentence that names a POSITIONS entry (P-N) states a decision of the curator. Build on a sentence without one, but do not cite it as a decision. Question a rule only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Most rules follow the team's later type papers (`Papers/`) over the specification's early text (P-26; `exploring.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. Where a rule changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`).
+
+A sentence that cites a ledger row states a known departure of one path from a bold rule. A fix can change it, so do not assert it as correct in a test. A sentence that opens "Until the switch-over" states a limit of the compiler's library. The limit ends when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, so do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`). If a change is not here, search FACTS and POSITIONS (`records.md`) before you call a disagreement a conflict. An old note, a team test and your training can be right about the team's walk and wrong here: the number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, and walk converts arguments.
+
+## Dispatch and overloading
+
+**Overloads may differ in their static parameters (P-45).** An example is `ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T`. The Working Draft forbids such pairs. A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance, not at one only.
+
+**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value of both domains has one instance of each generic type at each position, so those instances' static arguments are equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair where the equalities leave a static parameter free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.
+
+**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".

+**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. The interpreter's library declares `=` on pairs and triples only, so `(s, 1, 2, 3) = (t, 1, 2, 3)` falls back to `SEQV` and is `false`; row 923 holds the question of longer tuples. To compare by content, give the value object an `=`, or compare the parts. A string's `=` compares text. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library declares no `=` over `Any` and none on tuples. Its own `≣`, declared as `===`, compares strings and `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64` by `=`, not by bits or identity (row 908).

+## Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes
+
+**A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not Scala's `Nothing` (P-48).** The checker takes the intersection of its upper bounds, narrowed by the expected type. Under walk, a parameter whose bound names itself stays open, printed `OPEN`, as in `BoxU[\OPEN\]`. Every value passes `OPEN` itself. Where walk compares overloads, a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at `Bottom`: beside `pick(x: Any)`, `pick(x: (T,T))` takes no `(1, 2)`. Walk still gives `Bottom` to these parameters:
+
+- one with two bounds, neither below the other (row 591);
+- one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);
+- one that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (row 587).
+
+**Only the checker gives a call written as an argument the enclosing call's context (P-51).** If the enclosing call fails as written, the checker types the inner call again against each declaration's parameter type. So `takesBox64(mk())` compiles for `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]`. Walk gives an argument no expected type, so there `mk()` takes its bound (row 705). Under walk, write `mk[\ZZ64\]()`.
+
+**Three `where` forms are built (P-151).** Conditional extension is an `extends` entry with a `where` clause that binds no variable and states only constraints `T extends SomeTrait`. The type extends the parent only where they hold, as `List[\E\]` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`. The other two forms:
+
+- a condition of a function or method on its own static parameters, or of a method on its trait's, checked at a call;
+- a type variable of a `where` clause in a `comprises` clause, as `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`.
+
+The checker reads an `extends` entry with any other `where` clause as unconditional, without a message. Walk and the compiled runtime apply a conditional extension at every instance (row 774). Walk runs a dotted call that breaks a method's condition (row 777). The code generator accepts a declaration's own `where` clause but emits no code for it, so the compiled runtime does not check it. A compiled call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, dies at run time (row 867). `compiler.md` gives the checker's gaps.
+
+**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).
+
+**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. Such a call does not run compiled yet. Until the switch-over, compiled programs do not link `NatReflect`, which is part of the interpreter's library. After the switch-over, such a call still fails, for a second reason. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, so its `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size. A compiled call fails the JVM's verification if it passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected (row 307). This holds for a program's own trait too.
+
+## Numbers
+
+**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** The record calls this choice route A. Route C is the way not chosen: a checker rule under which the number types could nest again. The record still calls the number and order traits "the tower". That word does not mean that they nest.
+
+**A numeral converts where it stands (P-173).** A numeral's own type is `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]`, or `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` with a radix point (P-174). Its static arguments are the numeral's numbers: the digit count, the digits after the point, the radix, and the digits read as one integer. So `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`. Both types lie below `Numeral`, a sibling of the number types under `Number`. They exist only at compile time. No numeral value exists when a program runs, so a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares the same types and coercions (P-37), but its `RR64` and `RR32` take only a radix-point numeral, so a compiled program writes `3.0` there (row 442). A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`, and `(h = 0.5)` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the binding runs, with 'Type mismatch binding' and the numeral. Walk gives `Infinity` for the second (row 967). Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. Elsewhere includes an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, `Index` and an unbounded type parameter. So `n = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64`, and `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`. The default stays the value's type: for `x = 0.1`, `q: QQ = x` is refused. A type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default that holds them all. A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`, so `u: NN32 = n` is refused (P-173, P-40). Such a parameter of 2^31 or more is a `ZZ64` under walk, and raises an error on the compiled path (row 962).

+Write a numeral type only as the parameter type of a coercion or an operator. The checker refuses it as the type of a variable, a field or a return (P-174). A program's own number type receives a numeral through its own `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral)` or `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`. Its body reads the numeral's getters `digits`, `fractionDigits`, `radix` and `digitValue`. A negative constant, as `-3`, reaches it as the type's prefix `-` on the coercion's result for `3`, so a type without `-` refuses it. Until the switch-over, a compiled program writes `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` or `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)`. The coercion gives one value for each place where the numeral is written, and each run of that place reuses it. Without such a coercion, the type refuses a numeral. The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or a `Matrix` only at the eight number types; at a program's own number type they give a plain array. `interpreter.md` and `compiler.md` give the other departures from these rules.

It leaves alone the wrapping, saturating and bitwise operators, the shifts, a division by zero, an integer base at a negative exponent, and a result that can be `-0.0`. A folded comparison is a boolean. Any other result is one numeral, which converts as above or takes its default, or a quotient that is not whole, which stays `n / d` in lowest terms and defaults to a `QQ`. So `2147483647 + 1` is the `ZZ64` 2147483648, not an `IntegerOverflow`, `(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3)` is `true`, and under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`. `||` of string literals folds into one literal (P-171). A chain of `||` folds character literals too, if its first or second operand is a string literal. A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand: write `m: ZZ32 = 2147483647`, then `m + 1`, or `t: String = "ab"`, then `t || "c"`.
+
+**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts a value other than a numeral at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). The rule converts at a declared return type too, but walk does not (row 387). Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where the tied declarations differ only at the positions of the call's numerals, both paths read the numeral as its default.
+
+**An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter, as `x.asZZ32`: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The low-bits functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. On the fixed-width types, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, `narrow` and `widen` give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, `signed` and `unsigned` the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and `big` a `ZZ`. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. `ZZ` has only `big`, so for a `ZZ` value `z`, `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. Each `bitsAs…` getter equals `unsigned` or `signed`, as `bitsAsNN32` of a `ZZ32`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has only these getters: `asZZ` on each fixed-width type, `asZZ32` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, `asNN32` on `NN32`, and `asNN64` on `NN64`. It has no `big`, and of the low-bits functions only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349).
+
+**`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types, and the two numeral types, declares its own `asFloat` into `RR64`. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error, as for a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. To compare values across types at known types, write `asFloat(x) = y`. In generic code over `T extends Number`, declare your function once for each number type instead. A program may also declare its own number type below `Number` (P-160).

At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. No coercion carries a `ZZ64` into `RR64`, so convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.

+## Reductions and comprehensions
+
+A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.
+
+**A reduction's static argument depends on the path.** The checker does not infer it for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, whose bound names the parameter (row 731). Write it in every clause form, as `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Other reductions take their bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types. If that join is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1". Departures under walk:
+
+- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
+- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (row 717);
+- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).
+
+**A reduction without an identity lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction.** `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and the string reduction `BIG //` extend `AssociativeReduction[\R\]`, whose `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`. `BIG MAX` over a generator still answers `R`. Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one stops at its first join. The team's tests declare `simpleJoin` so: do not copy them.
+
+## Implementation limits
+
+**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). So walk runs programs that the checker refuses. Besides a `Boolean`, it takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. It refuses any other value. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition. The compiled path's own limits are in `compiler.md`.
+
+**Write every parameter type.** The compiled path refuses a parameter without a type, of a function, a method or a local function: "Missing parameter type for". Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.

+# What the revival changed in the team's Fortress
+
+This part gives the departures of revived Fortress from the team's Fortress, and from what you expect from Java, Scala, Haskell or Julia. The team left three forms that disagree: the specification, walk with the interpreter's library, and the compiled path with the compiler's library. The rules below resolve them. Read the part whole, after `SKILL.md`, before work.
+
+Each bold rule states the rule of this tree. A sentence that names a POSITIONS entry (P-N) states a decision of the curator. Build on a sentence without one, but do not cite it as a decision. Question a rule only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Most rules follow the team's later type papers (`Papers/`) over the specification's early text (P-26; `exploring.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. Where a rule changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`).
+
+A sentence that cites a ledger row states a known departure of one path from a bold rule. A fix can change it, so do not assert it as correct in a test. A sentence that opens "Until the switch-over" states a limit of the compiler's library. The limit ends when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, so do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`). If a change is not here, search FACTS and POSITIONS (`records.md`) before you call a disagreement a conflict. An old note, a team test and your training can be right about the team's walk and wrong here: the number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, and walk converts arguments.
+
+## Dispatch and overloading
+
+**Overloads may differ in their static parameters (P-45).** An example is `ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T`. The Working Draft forbids such pairs. A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance, not at one only.
+
+**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value of both domains has one instance of each generic type at each position, so those instances' static arguments are equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair where the equalities leave a static parameter free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.
+
+**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".
+
+**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk. For example, walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains only at a call (row 780).
+
+**Two functional methods with equivalent parameter types are duplicates, wherever `self` stands.** So the checker refuses `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` in a trait `S`. Abstract declarations count:
+
+- both paths refuse an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait;
+- both paths refuse an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, unless the object declares the method itself (P-149). The Scala language accepts it.
+
+The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (`SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"). An abstract functional method also counts for it. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's `+` between an array and a number, because a type can extend both the trait and `Number`, which has no `comprises` clause (P-160). Declare the trait `excludes { Number }`, or make it exclude arrays, `excludes { HasRank }`. Or declare the `+` in an object, not in a trait: an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, because no other type can extend it. Otherwise walk refuses the program at load: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker refuses such a pair in one component, but accepts it against the library's `+` (row 918). Give a trait with its own functional `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` the same fix: the library declares these in the same form.
+
+## Traits and objects
+
+**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk does not apply the rule: it runs such a type, and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, because it does not read them as excluding (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule "Not allowed": do not copy them.
+
+**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. So a generic trait need not be listed if every type below it is below a listed type, as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`. A Java `permits` list names each direct subtype; this clause need not. Read so, several declarations can together cover the meet of two overloads. At load, walk checks extenders only against the clauses of the program's main component (row 551).
+
+**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. To replace an inherited declaration at its own parameter types, declare it again without `override`. An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it. The checker checks that an overriding return type is a subtype. Walk refuses at load an `override` that, by this rule, overrides nothing, so a Java-style `override` in the library stops every program. Two departures: the checker accepts such an `override` (row 653), and the code generator refuses every `override` modifier (row 650).
+
+**An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies that together cover its parameter types (P-147).** It needs one body at those types, or several narrower bodies that cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk refuses at load an object without static parameters that leaves one uncovered. Walk skips this check for a generic object (row 665). Walk stops its search for a cover at limits that `interpreter.md` gives, and the checker at the same limits. The checker refuses a cover by several bodies where the abstract or a covering method has static parameters (row 725).
+
+**In a self-typed trait the checker types `self` as the trait met with the implementing type.** A trait `T` is self-typed if both conditions hold:
+
+- `T` has no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`;
+- `T` has a parameter `X` bounded by `T` itself, as `trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\]` (P-146), or by a self-typed trait `U[\X\]` that `T` extends, as `trait T[\X extends U[\X\]\] extends U[\X\]`.
+
+In `T`'s bodies, `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X`. So `floor(self): I = self` in `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` is valid without a cast. The checker refuses a type that extends `T[\A\]` and is not an `A`. A compiled body of `T` that returns `self` fails the JVM's verification when its class loads (row 695).
+
+When the checker applies the overloading rules to a method of `T`, `self` has the type `T[\X\]`, except in its test of whether two domains exclude each other. There `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X` (P-157). With this reading and the bounds that the test reads ("Dispatch and overloading"), the library's generic `+` and `-` between an array and a number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own. Walk reads `self` in the same way, so it loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component. Walk's load check, which is not the verdict ("Dispatch and overloading"), still refuses the pair in two cases:
+
+- `T` is self-typed only through another self-typed trait that it extends;
+- `T`'s method has static parameters of its own.
+
+**An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (P-156).** An indexed type is a type whose values `a[i]` subscripts, such as an array. Its index parameter is the static parameter that gives the type of `i`. In the library, and in your own generic over such a type, write `I extends Index`. Walk runs the code without the bound. The checker refuses it when it checks against the interpreter's library, as the count stage does (`compiler.md`). Of the integer types, only `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes `Index`. A numeral at a parameter of type `Index` takes its default, a `ZZ32`, so `f(3)` is valid for `f(x: Index)`. The Working Draft lets no trait type hold a tuple, but here a tuple whose element types are all `Index` types is an `Index`. So `m[i, j]` passes the pair `(i, j)` as one index. `Index` extends only `Any`, so such a tuple is still no `Object`. The empty tuple `()` is no `Index`. A function over `Index` and one over a tuple of `Index` types do not exclude each other. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `Index`, so a program that names it does not compile: write the bound only in code that runs under walk or is checked against the interpreter's library. Two departures:
+
+- the checker refuses a tuple expression at a parameter of type `Index`, but takes one at a parameter of type `I`, where `I extends Index` (row 805);
+- walk loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it (row 806).
+
+**Pairs and triples are ordered only where each element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`.** This holds for `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP`. Walk refuses another element type at the call, also where earlier elements decide, as `(1,()) < (2,())`. It also refuses numbers of two run-time types at one position, as `(1,2) < (1,2.5)` (row 511). Unordered deciding elements give `false`, or `Unordered` for `CMP`. The checker orders a `List[\E\]` only where `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`, so a list of `RR64` has no order there (P-154). Walk orders every list (row 774). A list's `=` stays element by element.
+
+**Where a type declares no `=`, `=` is strict equivalence, `SEQV` (P-168).** Strict equivalence is the operator `≣` (STRICTLY EQUIVALENT TO), written `SEQV` or `===` in ASCII. The operator `≡` (IDENTICAL TO, `EQV` or `EQUIV`) is a different one: logical equivalence on booleans. The interpreter's library declares it for no type, and walk stops on it (row 184): write `a <-> b`. The library's `=` over `Any` answers `a SEQV b`. `SEQV` follows the specification on both paths:
+
+- values of different types are never equivalent;
+- a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, an integer, a character or a boolean by its value, and a float by its bits;
+- a reference object, a string among them, is equivalent only to itself;
+- a function is equivalent to itself, but may be found unequal to another that behaves the same.
+
+So for a value object `V` without its own `=`, `V(s) = V(t)` is `false` where `s` and `t` are equal strings made by two computations. Two string literals of one text are one object (P-171). So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` and `V("ab") = V("ab")` are `true`. Two string literals joined by `||` fold into one ("Numbers"), so `("a" || "b") SEQV "ab"` is `true`. A float numeral converts where `RR64` is declared ("Numbers"), so `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed `RR64` 0.5. The interpreter's library declares `=` on pairs and triples only, so `(s, 1, 2, 3) = (t, 1, 2, 3)` falls back to `SEQV` and is `false`; row 923 holds the question of longer tuples. To compare by content, give the value object an `=`, or compare the parts. A string's `=` compares text. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library declares no `=` over `Any` and none on tuples. Its own `≣`, declared as `===`, compares strings and `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64` by `=`, not by bits or identity (row 908).
+
+## Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes
+
+**A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not Scala's `Nothing` (P-48).** The checker takes the intersection of its upper bounds, narrowed by the expected type. Under walk, a parameter whose bound names itself stays open, printed `OPEN`, as in `BoxU[\OPEN\]`. Every value passes `OPEN` itself. Where walk compares overloads, a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at `Bottom`: beside `pick(x: Any)`, `pick(x: (T,T))` takes no `(1, 2)`. Walk still gives `Bottom` to these parameters:
+
+- one with two bounds, neither below the other (row 591);
+- one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);
+- one that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (row 587).
+
+**Only the checker gives a call written as an argument the enclosing call's context (P-51).** If the enclosing call fails as written, the checker types the inner call again against each declaration's parameter type. So `takesBox64(mk())` compiles for `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]`. Walk gives an argument no expected type, so there `mk()` takes its bound (row 705). Under walk, write `mk[\ZZ64\]()`.
+
+**Three `where` forms are built (P-151).** Conditional extension is an `extends` entry with a `where` clause that binds no variable and states only constraints `T extends SomeTrait`. The type extends the parent only where they hold, as `List[\E\]` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`. The other two forms:
+
+- a condition of a function or method on its own static parameters, or of a method on its trait's, checked at a call;
+- a type variable of a `where` clause in a `comprises` clause, as `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`.
+
+The checker reads an `extends` entry with any other `where` clause as unconditional, without a message. Walk and the compiled runtime apply a conditional extension at every instance (row 774). Walk runs a dotted call that breaks a method's condition (row 777). The code generator accepts a declaration's own `where` clause but emits no code for it, so the compiled runtime does not check it. A compiled call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, dies at run time (row 867). `compiler.md` gives the checker's gaps.
+
+**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).
+
+**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. Such a call does not run compiled yet. Until the switch-over, compiled programs do not link `NatReflect`, which is part of the interpreter's library. After the switch-over, such a call still fails, for a second reason. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, so its `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size. A compiled call fails the JVM's verification if it passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected (row 307). This holds for a program's own trait too.
+
+## Numbers
+
+**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** The record calls this choice route A. Route C is the way not chosen: a checker rule under which the number types could nest again. The record still calls the number and order traits "the tower". That word does not mean that they nest.
+
+**A numeral converts where it stands (P-173).** A numeral's own type is `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]`, or `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` with a radix point (P-174). Its static arguments are the numeral's numbers: the digit count, the digits after the point, the radix, and the digits read as one integer. So `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`. Both types lie below `Numeral`, a sibling of the number types under `Number`. They exist only at compile time. No numeral value exists when a program runs, so a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares the same types and coercions (P-37), but its `RR64` and `RR32` take only a radix-point numeral, so a compiled program writes `3.0` there (row 442). A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, and `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the binding runs, with 'Type mismatch binding' and the numeral. Walk gives `Infinity` for the second (row 967). Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. Elsewhere includes an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, `Index` and an unbounded type parameter. So `n = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64`, and `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`. The default stays the value's type: for `x = 0.1`, `q: QQ = x` is refused. A type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default that holds them all. A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`, so `u: NN32 = n` is refused (P-173, P-40). Such a parameter of 2^31 or more is a `ZZ64` under walk, and raises an error on the compiled path (row 962).
+
+Write a numeral type only as the parameter type of a coercion or an operator. The checker refuses it as the type of a variable, a field or a return (P-174). A program's own number type receives a numeral through its own `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral)` or `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`. Its body reads the numeral's getters `digits`, `fractionDigits`, `radix` and `digitValue`. A negative constant, as `-3`, reaches it as the type's prefix `-` on the coercion's result for `3`, so a type without `-` refuses it. Until the switch-over, a compiled program writes `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` or `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)`. The coercion gives one value for each place where the numeral is written, and each run of that place reuses it. Without such a coercion, the type refuses a numeral. The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or a `Matrix` only at the eight number types; at a program's own number type they give a plain array. `interpreter.md` and `compiler.md` give the other departures from these rules.
+
+**An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker, on both paths (P-173).** The fold covers the arithmetic operators, `^` up to the exponent 4096, `MIN`, `MAX`, the comparisons, and `DIV`, `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD`, `LCM`, `CHOOSE` and `MINMAX` over integers. It leaves alone the wrapping, saturating and bitwise operators, the shifts, a division by zero, an integer base at a negative exponent, and a result that can be `-0.0`. A folded comparison is a boolean. Any other result is one numeral, which converts as above or takes its default, or a quotient that is not whole, which stays `n / d` in lowest terms and defaults to a `QQ`. So `2147483647 + 1` is the `ZZ64` 2147483648, not an `IntegerOverflow`, `(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3)` is `true`, and under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`. `||` of string literals folds into one literal (P-171). A chain of `||` folds character literals too, if its first or second operand is a string literal. A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand: write `m: ZZ32 = 2147483647`, then `m + 1`, or `t: String = "ab"`, then `t || "c"`.
+
+**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts a value other than a numeral at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). The rule converts at a declared return type too, but walk does not (row 387). Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". Where the tied declarations differ only at the positions of the call's numerals, both paths read the numeral as its default.
+
+**An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter, as `x.asZZ32`: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The low-bits functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. On the fixed-width types, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, `narrow` and `widen` give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, `signed` and `unsigned` the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and `big` a `ZZ`. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. `ZZ` has only `big`, so for a `ZZ` value `z`, `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. Each `bitsAs…` getter equals `unsigned` or `signed`, as `bitsAsNN32` of a `ZZ32`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has only these getters: `asZZ` on each fixed-width type, `asZZ32` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, `asNN32` on `NN32`, and `asNN64` on `NN64`. It has no `big`, and of the low-bits functions only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349).
+
+**`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types, and the two numeral types, declares its own `asFloat` into `RR64`. So generic code over `T extends Number` can call on a `T` no method or operator that the number types declare, `asFloat` among them. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error, as for a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. To compare values across types at known types, write `asFloat(x) = y`. In generic code over `T extends Number`, declare your function once for each number type instead. A program may also declare its own number type below `Number` (P-160).
+
+**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).
+
+**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. No coercion carries a `ZZ64` into `RR64`, so convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.
+
+## Reductions and comprehensions
+
+A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.
+
+**A reduction's static argument depends on the path.** The checker does not infer it for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, whose bound names the parameter (row 731). Write it in every clause form, as `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Other reductions take their bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types. If that join is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1". Departures under walk:
+
+- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
+- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (row 717);
+- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).
+
+**A reduction without an identity lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction.** `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and the string reduction `BIG //` extend `AssociativeReduction[\R\]`, whose `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`. `BIG MAX` over a generator still answers `R`. Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one stops at its first join. The team's tests declare `simpleJoin` so: do not copy them.
+
+## Implementation limits
+
+**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). So walk runs programs that the checker refuses. Besides a `Boolean`, it takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. It refuses any other value. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition. The compiled path's own limits are in `compiler.md`.
+
+**Write every parameter type.** The compiled path refuses a parameter without a type, of a function, a method or a local function: "Missing parameter type for". Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.

Its static arguments are the numeral's numbers: the digit count, the digits after the point, the radix, and the digits read as one integer. So `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`. Both types lie below `Numeral`, a sibling of the number types under `Number`. They exist only at compile time. No numeral value exists when a program runs, so a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares the same types and coercions (P-37), but its `RR64` and `RR32` take only a radix-point numeral, so a compiled program writes `3.0` there (row 442). A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, and `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the binding runs, with 'Type mismatch binding' and the numeral. Walk gives `Infinity` for the second (row 967). Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. Elsewhere includes an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, `Index` and an unbounded type parameter. So `n = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64`, and `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`. A program's own number type takes a numeral through a coercion generic over the numbers: `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\])`, or `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\])` with a radix point. Its body reads the numbers as `ZZ` values of any size, so a `ZZ32` field takes `v.asZZ32`, as in `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = Byte(v.asZZ32)` for `value object Byte(b: ZZ32)` (P-173, P-40). Until the switch-over, a compiled program writes `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` or `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)`. The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or a `Matrix` only at the eight number types; at a program's own number type they give a plain array. `interpreter.md` and `compiler.md` give the other departures from these rules.
+
+**An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker, on both paths (P-173).** The fold covers the arithmetic operators, `^` up to the exponent 4096, `MIN`, `MAX`, the comparisons, and `DIV`, `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD`, `LCM`, `CHOOSE` and `MINMAX` over integers. It leaves alone the wrapping, saturating and bitwise operators, the shifts, a division by zero, an integer base at a negative exponent, and a result that can be `-0.0`. A folded comparison is a boolean. Any other result is one numeral, which converts as above or takes its default, or a quotient that is not whole, which stays `n / d` in lowest terms and defaults to a `QQ`. So `2147483647 + 1` is the `ZZ64` 2147483648, not an `IntegerOverflow`, `(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3)` is `true`, and under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`. `||` of string literals folds into one literal (P-171). A chain of `||` folds character literals too, if its first or second operand is a string literal. A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand: write `m: ZZ32 = 2147483647`, then `m + 1`, or `t: String = "ab"`, then `t || "c"`.

For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. No coercion carries a `ZZ64` into `RR64`, so convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.

+
+A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.

+**A reduction's static argument depends on the path.** The checker does not infer it for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, whose bound names the parameter (row 731). Write it in every clause form, as `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Other reductions take their bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types. If that join is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1". Departures under walk:

+- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
+- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (row 717);

Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one stops at its first join. The team's tests declare `simpleJoin` so: do not copy them.
+
+## Implementation limits
+
+**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). So walk runs programs that the checker refuses. Besides a `Boolean`, it takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. It refuses any other value. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition. The compiled path's own limits are in `compiler.md`.
+
+**Write every parameter type.** The compiled path refuses a parameter without a type, of a function, a method or a local function: "Missing parameter type for". Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.
